justification: All three provided articles concern CHRNA1 (muscle acetylcholine receptor alpha-subunit) microsatellite associations with autoimmune myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder, not epilepsy (PMIDs 7910962, 8738961, 9237805). None reports any epilepsy phenotype, seizures, or CNS involvement, and the muscle-type alpha1 subunit is not a neuronal receptor subunit implicated in these data. There is therefore no genetic, functional, or expression evidence linking CHRNA1 variation to epilepsy in this literature set. A small residual probability is allotted to "hypothesized" only because of the general cholinergic-receptor family biology, which is not supported by any article here.

justification: No article in this set reports KCNC1 variants in epilepsy patients; the only human mutation screening (PMID 9041816, 9445488) tested KCNC1 as a positional candidate for Usher syndrome type IC and found no coding mutations, which is irrelevant to epilepsy. The remaining literature is biophysical/pharmacological characterization of Kv3.1 channels in heterologous systems (PMIDs 7517498, 7696467, 7696472, 9222902) and expression work showing Kv3.1 in fast-spiking parvalbumin GABAergic interneurons and other high-frequency-firing neurons (PMIDs 1432046, 10531438, 10414968), biology plausibly relevant to cortical excitability. Importantly, the Kv3.1-null mouse was explicitly tested and did NOT show increased spontaneous seizures (PMID 9037088; see also 10863995), i.e., the animal model provides negative rather than supportive evidence. Thus the link rests only on general excitability biology and an expectation that was experimentally refuted, placing this between Hypothesized and Novel, with no human genetic support for Existing or Established.
